Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, and dear friends, it is a pleasure to join you today on behalf of the Secretary-General and to welcome you to this international meeting on victim assistance and environmental remediation. The Secretary-General, who is travelling at the moment, sends his warm greetings to all participants and his best wishes for a productive and substantive meeting. I would like to express my sincere appreciation to the Governments of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan for their leadership in bringing us together for this important discussion. I would also like to thank all participants for being with us today, especially those representatives of affected communities, the victims of poisonous legacy of nuclear use and testing. And I welcome the members of international organizations, civil society, academia, and the scientific community. I look forward to hearing your expert views. The General Assembly has provided us with a clear purpose for today's meeting, to exchange experiences and views, advance international cooperation, and identify practical ways to support people and communities affected by the use and testing of nuclear weapons. The consequences of nuclear weapons do not end when an explosion is over. As the enduring suffering of the hibakusha, the survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the legacy of more than 2,000 nuclear tests around the world make clear, the effects of nuclear weapons persist for decades and across generations. These consequences affect human health and well-being. They disrupt livelihoods, communities, and traditional ways of life. They leave lasting impacts on land, water, and the broader environment. Addressing these consequences cannot be achieved through short-term measures. It requires sustained national efforts, appropriate expertise and resources, and effective international cooperation. Allow me to highlight a few practical considerations as we begin our discussions today. First, affected people and communities must remain at the center of our efforts. Their experiences are essential to understanding both the nature of the harm they have suffered and the assistance that can make a meaningful difference in their lives. This means listening to affected communities and ensuring their meaningful participation in decisions that concern them. Their knowledge and expertise can help identify priorities, improve the design of assistance, and ensure that measures taken respond to actual needs and circumstances. Victim assistance can take different forms depending on national circumstances and the needs of those affected. It may include access to appropriate health care, long-term health monitoring, psychological support, as well as measures addressing social and economic consequences. No single model will apply everywhere. What matters is that assistance is accessible, responsive to identified needs, and sustained over time. Second, Environmental remediation also requires a long-term approach. States and communities affected by nuclear weapons use and testing need reliable information about environmental impacts and access to the scientific technical expertise necessary to determine appropriate responses. This may involve assessing affected areas, monitoring environmental conditions, and identifying measures that can reduce risks and support the safe and sustainable use of land and natural resources. Here, international cooperation has a particularly important role to play. Not every affected state has access to all the technical capacities or resources it may require. Sharing scientific knowledge, expertise and lessons learned can strengthen national efforts and help ensure that existing experience is put to wider use. Third, we should make better use of the considerable experience and capacities that already exist. Governments, affected communities International organizations, scientific institutions, academia and civil society have accumulated important knowledge throughout the nuclear age. Some states have developed extensive experience in providing health and social support to affected populations. Others have undertaken environmental monitoring and remediation activities. International and regional organizations possess expertise that can contribute to these efforts, while affected communities themselves hold knowledge that cannot be obtained from scientific or technical assessments alone. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, TPNW, has also provided an important framework through its articles on victim assistance, environmental remediation, and international cooperation and assistance. States parties and relevant stakeholders continue to develop practical approaches to their implementation. A key challenge before us now is how to bring these different forms of knowledge and capacity together. International cooperation can help strengthen national capacities through training, technical assistance, information sharing and institutional partnerships. Where resources are limited, financial assistance can also be important in enabling affected states and communities to undertake and sustain necessary activities and initiatives. Fourth and finally, our efforts must be sustainable. The impacts we are discussing today are often measured in decades, not years. Responses therefore cannot depend solely on individual projects or temporary initiatives. Continuity matters. National institutions need the capacity to preserve knowledge and experience. Scientific and health information may need to be maintained over long periods. At the multilateral level, sustained cooperation and institutional engagement are equally important to ensure that expertise, assistance and lessons learned remain available over time. Communities need confidence that support will not disappear when a particular project or funding cycle comes to an end. International cooperation should support this longer term perspective. This meeting provides a valuable opportunity to examine these questions together. I therefore encourage all participants to focus on concrete experience throughout today's discussions. What approaches have worked? What challenges continue to prevent effective assistance? Where are the most significant gaps in national capacity? What forms of international cooperation have proved useful? And where could better coordination, stronger partnerships, or additional resources make a tangible difference? I also encourage us to listen carefully to the voices of affected communities represented here today. Their participation is not only important in principle, it is essential to understand where existing approaches are succeeding, where they are falling short, and what priorities should guide further efforts. We're not starting from zero. There is significant experience to draw upon, knowledge to share, and expertise that can be mobilized. There is also growing international recognition that addressing the humanitarian and environmental consequences of nuclear weapons requires sustained attention and practical cooperation. I hope that this meeting will help identify areas where international efforts can translate, above all, into tangible support for affected people and communities, and into effective environmental remediation. I wish you a productive and constructive meeting. I thank you very much for your attention.

Thank you for this opportunity to speak before you. I am Hibakusha, a survivor of atomic bombing of Nagasaki in 1945. I was inside a house located 2.9 kilometers from the hypocenter when the bomb exploded. then I was only one year and 10 months old and have no memories of that day myself. So I am sharing the story as told to me by my mother. Thanks to the terrain of Nagasaki, which is surrounded by mountains, I survived without suffering any direct injuries or burns. The blast destroyed all the furniture, doors, and windows inside the house. The earthen walls crumbled and debris piled 30 centimeters high on the tatami mats. My mother saw a procession of chocolate-colored people, indistinguishable as men or women, staggering down the mountains. mountain pass from the epicenter like a line of ants. Carrying me on her back, she went to the well in the backyard where she washed the wounds and people who had come seeking help and water using old clothes as temporary bandages. On the vacant lot next door, bodies loaded into garbage carts were cremated every day. My mother, who had been sent from our neighborhood to help at the makeshift aid station, fainted at the sight of people with unspeakable injuries and burns. Her subsequent last task was to brush off and remove the worming maggots around the wounds of the victims lying on the floor. Later on, she would occasionally speak of those days when she felt as she had lost her humanity. Every August, she felt that same smell return. She used to say, people weren't born just to be burned like trash. Beneath that mushroom cloud were people, each with a name, loved ones, family, and lives that matters more than anything else. Under U.S. occupation, strict censorship was imposed on press reports about the atomic bombings, and the hibakusha were never informed of the cause of the physical and mental suffering and grief. As a result, they were forced to remain silent amid the discrimination and prejudice they faced from society. In September 1945, Brigadier General Thomas Farrell, deputy head of the US Manhattan Project, visited Japan. At the press conference, he made remarks to the effect that in Hiroshima, those who were doomed to die had already died, and there were no one suffering from radiation. This led to the closure of all temporary relief stations. People died without knowing why they were dying. And the number of deaths spread in concentric circles from the hypocenter. By the end of December 1945, about 140,000 people had died in Hiroshima and 70,000 in Nagasaki. 65% of them were children, women, and the elderly. And only 4% died attended by their families. Many were burned like garbage, their identities unknown. Those cremated by their families may have been the fortunate ones. The hibakusha who survived 70 years under US occupation endured a forced silence, grappling with survivor's guilt, illness, and poverty, and had to give up many of their dreams. Abandoned by the governments of Japan and the United States, they lived under this forced silence. In 1954, following the Bikini incident, a hydrogen bomb test conducted by the United States at Bikini Atoll, the Japanese public, having come to understand the dangers and the horrors of radiation, launched a signature campaign for total ban on nuclear weapons. The movement spread like wildfire across the nation, gathering more than 30 million signatures and ultimately leading to the convening of the first world conference against A and H bombs. Hibakusha, who had remained silent until then, came forward hoping their voices would be heard. Eleven years after the atomic bombings, in 1956, the Japan Confederation of A and H Bomb Sufferers Organization, Nihon Hidankyo, was established. The message to the world, its founding declaration proclaimed, We have reassured our will to save humanity from its crisis through the lessons learned from our experiences, while at the same time saving ourselves. Hibakusha's physical and emotional wounds have not yet healed, and putting their experiences into words might draw them back to that time. but their noble pledge that no one else should ever have to go through the same suffering moves me deeply. Saving oneself meant not only receiving aid but also gaining strength and finding salvation by taking on that mission through the movement. And today, we are here to discuss assistance for nuclear victims and environmental remediation. The core demands of Nihon Hidankyo's 70-year movement have been the abolition of nuclear weapons and the state compensation for the atomic damage. Through our own struggle, we have achieved an attachment of the following through laws. First one, A-bomb Sufferers Medical Care Law, March 1957, the law established the hibakusha certificate system proving health examination for the certified hibakusha. Second one, law concerning special measures for A-bomb sufferers, May 1968. The survey on the Ibaksha conducted for the first time by the Ministry of Health in 1965 revealed their difficult economic situation leading to the enactment of this law proving several kind of allowance for them. And the third one, law concerning relief to Atomic Bomb Survivors, A-bomb Survivors Relief Law, December 1994. This law combined the two previous laws while denying, while continuing to deny the state compensation to those killed by the atomic bombs. The law remained limited to the framework of Social Security measures for the survivors. The foremost victims, foremost victims were those who were killed, those who were unable to return home within two weeks of the atomic bombings, such as evacuated orphans, and those who returned from the battlefield only to find their entire families had perished were unable to obtain the hibakusha certificate and were therefore all excluded from receiving benefits. Consequently, Nihon Hidankyo continues to demand a new law that can truly be called a hibakusha aid law. Why does Nihon Hidankyo demand state compensation rather than social security? It is because the war was started by the state. The Japanese government stands that citizens must endure the loss of their lives, physical bodies, livelihood, and mental well-being resulting from that war amounts to a refusal to take responsibility for future wars, which is absolutely unacceptable even today. Nihon Hidankyo continues its struggle to seek revisions to the current law. Regarding the global consequences of nuclear damage, responsibility lies with the countries that use nuclear weapons, their allies, and those that repeatedly conducted nuclear tests. I propose that we begin this conference by learning about and empathizing with the humanitarian consequences of the use of nuclear weapons, an absolute evil that indiscriminately killed more than 201,000 people in an instant, as if it were our own personal experience. Once nuclear weapons are used, there is no such thing as a priority for aid. No country or international organization has the means to provide relief. Doctors and nurses would also be exposed to radiation. What direction is the world with more than 12,000 nuclear weapons heading? What would humanity hope for in a world where everything has been destroyed? Saving the world from its crisis in turn means saving ourselves. Nuclear weapons are neither a force for justice nor the source of power. Today, we are witnessing first-hand the reality that even possessing nuclear weapons cannot bring an end to war. This is because we know there is something that should never have been used and must never be used. We must not create any more global hibakusha. For 70 years, we have continued to speak out because we do not want anyone in the world to go through the same experiences that we have. We earnestly hope that the wisdom of humanity will be brought together through the United Nations so that the feeling, appeals, and efforts of the hibakusha will not be in vain. No more war. No more hibakusha. Thank you very much.

Then France's more Aurora test site in the Pacific Ocean fell silent and in 1996 China's test site in the Lob Nor desert was shut down the world had heard of semipalatinsk yes testing was halted but nuclear arsenals still continue to grow the international situation is becoming more tense flash points are turning into entire volatile regions If radicals were to gain access to one of the world's nuclear arsenals, the whole earth would go up in flames. On August 29, 1949, the first Soviet nuclear explosion shook the Semipalatinsk test site. Over the next 40 years, At least 468 nuclear tests would be conducted here. Their combined yield would exceed the power of the Hiroshima bomb by two and a half thousand times. More than 1.3 million people would later be officially recognized as victims. One of them would be a boy born 19 years later. On July 18, 1968, a son was born to Teltai and Rimzhan Kuyukov in the village of Yagindybulak, Karaganda region. Before him, his mother had lost two boys, neither lived past their first year. Karabek survived, but he was born without both arms, a consequence of radiation from the test site. His mother prayed for only one thing, that he would live. And he did, against every prediction. At the age of six, his father took him to Leningrad, to the Institute of Prosthetics. A boarding school on the banks of the Neva River, near the cruiser Aurora, became his home for many years. There he learned to write with his foot, There he designed the school's wall newspapers. One day, he saw a man without arms painting with a brush held between his teeth. If he can do it, so can I. My feet are my hands, the boy told himself. That was the beginning of his journey as an artist. In 1987, After completing his studies in Zagorsk, near Moscow, Karabek returned to Kazakhstan. He was denied admission to an art school. The rector was unwilling to take responsibility. So he taught himself, studying library art albums and textbooks. His sister, Saule, stretched and primed his canvases. Then came a call from a museum. His first paintings had been purchased and taken to Germany. The payment was 19 times greater than his disability pension. It was a sign. His art mattered to people. A turning point came at a museum in Simi, where children who died as a result of radiation exposure are preserved in glass jars. I could have been one of them, the artist realized. and he made a vow to become the voice of those who could not speak for themselves. He joined the Nevada Semipalatinsk Anti-Nuclear Movement. For more than 35 years, the movement has united those who fight for a world free of nuclear weapons and preserve the memory of the consequences of nuclear testing. Karipbek collected the stories of 250 families with children affected by radiation, and organized charity exhibitions across the country and around the world. On August 29, 1991, the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site was closed forever. His paintings have been exhibited in the United States and Dubai. A painting featuring a falcon was presented to Jean-Claude Van Damme. Another of his works was carried by a mountaineer to the summit of Denali, the highest peak in North America. He also endured his greatest personal loss. In 2010, within the span of eight months, he lost both his father and his mother. Yet he never gave up. Today, he lives in Karaganda with his sister Saule, his guardian angel. "People call us disabled," says Karibek Kuyukov, "but our abilities are not limited." An artist born without arms who became the voice of nuclear test victims, he proved one simple truth. The only real limits exist not in the body, but in the human mind.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. We thank you for convening this meeting, and we recognize the work of Kazakhstan and Kiribati in developing this initiative. We're also grateful for the statements made by the USG Nakamitsu and the emotional words of Madam Wada and Mr. Yubov. The launching of the atomic bombs by the United States on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki led to the death and wounding of more than 200,000 people who died instantaneously over the course of a few months. This was one of the most abominable horrors of the war suffered by humanity. The members of many families are still suffering congenital failures because of the environmental pollution and other ongoing ecological damage passed on from one generation to the next. Productive economic activity has been damaged and, since then, natural areas have been changed as a result of detonations and the impact of radioactive material. The human and environmental damage caused by the use or testing of nuclear weapons is indiscriminate, uncontrollable, irreversible, goes through generations and persists over time, including its general capacity to produce radioactive pollution. In a context where the government of the United States is attempting to impose peace through force, the security of all peoples is at risk. It's ironic that it is that same government which, in a totally unjustified way, states that Cuba is a threat to its national security. has reinforced to unprecedented levels the economic, commercial and financial blockade, including a cruel energy freeze over the last eight months, and is threatening direct military action against my country. Cuba reaffirms its commitment to peace and to a world free of nuclear weapons based on cooperation, solidarity and absolute respect for the principles and purposes of the United Nations Charter and for international law. Mr. President, the total elimination of all nuclear weapons is the only absolute guarantee to prevent their use or their testing and all of the humanitarian, environmental and material damage that goes with that. This firm conviction is what led to the adoption and entry into force of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. This is the first international legal instrument which, in the area of nuclear disarmament, categorically prohibits nuclear weapons and includes humanitarian issues in its purposes and principles. and for the first time the TPNW clauses reflect the growing international concern about the humanitarian and environmental dimensions of the possible use or testing of nuclear weapons based on evidence gathered by members of the international community over many years. The provisions contained in Article 6 contain an explicit reference to medical psychological care and economic and social reinsertion of the victims without discrimination. This element refers to the importance that TPNW attaches to the importance of human beings. Cuba would call for universalisation of ratification of this treaty, an indispensable step in order to ensure its implementation, particularly with regard to assistance to victims and to clear up the areas that have been polluted, particularly paying attention to communities affected by the use or the testing of nuclear weapons and respecting the sovereignty of every state. My country recognizes the important role of the structures of the Preparatory Committee for the Organization for the Complete Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, particularly its international data system and its international monitoring system with more than 300 sites around the world. Its work in assisting in the dismantling of former installations for nuclear testing and its analysis of the radiation to detect the presence of fissile material in the areas affected makes a direct contribution to assistance activities for victims and environmental remediation. As part of the 30th anniversary of the opening of the Test Ban Treaty, we would call upon all states that have not yet done so to ratify this without delay. The complementarity between the TPNW and the other treaty is a real possibility to move to concrete action and to settle a historic debt with all human beings who suffer the scourges of war. As part of the first region, densely populated region of the planet that has been declared a zone free of nuclear weapons and proclaimed as a zone of peace, Cuba can state that nuclear disarmament is a question of human survival. Thank you very much.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Cuba for his statement and one word addressed to the Co-Chairs. I now give the floor to the representative of Costa Rica to be followed by the representative of Kazakhstan.

Co-Chairs, Costa Rica recognises the work and commitment of Kazakhstan, Kiribati and the secretariat in organising and convening this meeting. More than 80 years after the beginning of nuclear war, its victims continue to be with us and tell us about the consequences in their bodies and their communities. and in their lands. More than 2,000 nuclear tests have contaminated the environment and led to intergenerational effects in terms of health and development. Recognizing this legacy is indispensable, but that's not enough. Our responsibility is to transform that knowledge into assistance, remediation and justice. And in this regard, Costa Rica would make the following points. Firstly, We must place victims and affected communities at the centre of our efforts. Assistance should fully address the damage caused medical and psychological care, rehabilitation, social inclusion and economic inclusion, and recovery of the economic means for subsistence. The knowledge of the victims should also be taken into account when we are designing, implementing and assessing policies that relate to them. The discussions as part of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons for a trust fund to help victims and to provide for environmental remediation would move from moral statements about the victims to a dialogue on instruments that really are able to produce tangible results. Secondly, assistance should also correspond to scientific evidence. The effects of radiation, ionizing radiation, are not uniform and that is seen in the various studies that have been carried out and the risks are higher for women and children. A fair response does not mean offering identical assistance to all of the victims, but what it does mean is responding in different ways to different levels of damage, and therefore assistance programmes must be inclusive and sensitive to gender and to age. And thirdly, protecting people also means remediating their environment. Nuclear pollution for decades can contaminate, pollute water and food and other means of subsistence and stop people returning to their lands. Environmental remediation, therefore, is inseparable from the protection of human rights, from sustainable development and our responsibility to protect future generations. However, International solidarity should not be understood as a substitute for accountability. Resolution 7960 recognises that the responsibility to address the damage caused by the use or the testing of nuclear weapons falls on the shoulders of those states that carried out those tests or used those weapons in accordance with international law. And we can also make a cooperation through technical and financial cooperation according to our capacity in helping states and communities that have been affected. Finally, The information is also a form of reparations. The states affected need access to scientific and technical information on exposure, contamination and its consequences. The transparency and exchange of data and access to relevant archival data is essential for repairing the damage that has been caused and to provide effective remediation. Co-chairs. A couple of days ago we commemorated the 30th anniversary of the closing of a nuclear testing site, and that also reminded us that our legacies don't have to determine our futures. This meeting gives us the opportunity. to make progress and move from memory to action and to build a framework for cooperation that will provide effective protection. The responsibility to provide a remediation in the areas that have been marked by nuclear weapons should be at the forefront of our minds. Thank you.

I thank the representative of Costa Rica for the statement. I now give the floor to the Director General of the Department for International Security of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, to be followed by Indonesia.

Thank you. Co-chairs, Excellencies, distinguished representatives of affected communities, colleagues, Kazakhstan welcomes the convening of this international meeting pursuant to the General Assembly resolution 79/60 and 80/56. We also thank the Secretary-General, the President of the General Assembly and UNODA for organizing it. We particularly welcome the participation of affected communities, survivors, scientists, civil society, academia and relevant international organizations. And here I would like to commend the powerful statement delivered by Ms. Masaki Wada and Mr. Karibek Uyukov, by those who personally suffered from the consequences of nuclear weapon use and test. Your experience, courage, and the important messages you have conveyed to the world are deeply inspiring and give us hope for the future free of nuclear weapons. And for Kazakhstan, this is a matter of direct national experience. Between 1949 and 1989, 456 nuclear tests were conducted at the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site. Nearly one and a half million people were affected. and extensive territories were exposed to radioactive contamination. The closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site on August 29, 1991 ended nuclear testing on its territory, but it did not end its consequences. Affected people continue to face health, psychological, social, economic, and environmental harms. Some of these consequences extend across generations and require sustained national action and international cooperation. Kazakhstan has undertaken several measures on national level to provide medical and social support, conduct scientific research, monitor affected territories, and advance their rehabilitation. In 1992, Kazakhstan adopted the law that established radiation risk zone around the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site and provided social protection based on residents' exposure and place of residence. The state scientific automated medical register established in 2002 records victims and their descendants radiation doses and health outcomes. Government funded research programs from 1991 to 2019 examined radiation related health effects, medical and social consequences, risk to descendants, environmental impacts and methods of treatment, rehabilitation, prevention. In July 2023, Kazakhstan established the Simplifying Zone of Nuclear Safety to restrict access to highly contaminated land, rehabilitate affected areas, transfer relatively clean land to public ownership, and conduct continuous radiation and environmental monitoring with 3.5 billion Tenge allocated until 2026. General Assembly Resolution 78/142 provides an important framework for international cooperation on human and ecological rehabilitation and economic development of the Semipalatinsk region. Kazakhstan's experience points to several priorities. First, affected individuals and communities must remain central to decision-making. Their need, experience and knowledge should inform the design, implementation and evaluation of assistance and remediation programs. Second, victim assistance should be comprehensive, accessible, non-discriminatory and responsive to age and gender. Third, environmental remediation should be based on sound scientific evidence. And fourth, access to relevant information is indispensable. and also it called to states who is in position to do so to provide appropriate technical and financial assistance. Dear colleagues, the TPNW provides an important framework for this work through Article 6 and 7. Together with Kiribati, Kazakhstan serves as a co-chair of the informal working group on victim assistance, environmental remediation and international cooperation and assistance. On August 3, earlier this year, the co-chair submitted their report on possible guidelines, technical provisions, and terms of reference for the International Trust Fund for Victims Assistance and Environmental Remediation from the consequences of nuclear weapons use and testing. The report recommends that state parties commence a formal process towards establishing the fund with detailed terms of reference to be negotiated by adoption by fourth meeting of state parties. It recommends that the fund be established with the United Nations consistent with the United Nations rules and procedures and administered by UNODA with the Committee of State Parties providing oversight and recommendation on projects. Under the proposed approach, contributions would be voluntary with eligibility criteria to be determined by State Parties. The fund could support projects addressing medical, psychological, socio-economic, cultural and environmental harms. The co-chairs also recommend that affect communities and relevant experts participate at the invitation of State Parties throughout the Fund's work, including in the design and review of projects. These recommendations remain subject to consideration and decision by State Parties. While the terms of reference are being negotiated, the report also proposes consideration of a database to match requests for assistance with available financial, technical and scientific support. The proposed fund would be one mechanism for implementing Article 6 and 7. It should complement national programs and broader international cooperation, not replace them. Kazakhstan encourage this meeting to produce practical series of recommendations focused on nationally led assessments, meaningful community participation, access to relevant information, coordinated technical assistance, and sustainable financing. Kazakhstan stands ready to continue working with all partners to advance effective victim assistance, environmental remediation, and international cooperation. I thank you.

I thank the Director-General of Kazakhstan for his statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Indonesia to be followed by the representative of Philippines. Indonesia, you have the floor.

Co-chairs, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, my delegation acknowledges the work of Kazakhstan and Kiribati in convening this important meeting. We welcome the opportunity to advance international efforts on victim assistance and environmental remediation for states affected by the use and testing of nuclear weapons. The legacy of nuclear weapons use and testing remains a profound humanitarian and environmental challenge. More than 2,000 nuclear explosive tests have been conducted worldwide, leaving lasting impacts on human health, livelihoods, ecosystems and socio-economic development. Many affected communities continue to face the consequences of contamination, displacement and intergenerational harm decades after these tests took place. My delegation expresses its solidarity with all States and peoples affected by the use and testing of nuclear weapons and would like to underline three points. First, we recognize the urgent need to strengthen international cooperation to support victims, address health and environmental consequences, and assist affected states in building the technical and institutional capacities necessary for long-term remediation efforts. Second, states that have used or tested nuclear weapons bear a particular responsibility to address the resulting humanitarian and environmental harm consistent with international law. In this context, we encourage the sharing of relevant scientific and technical information, as well as the provision of adequate assistance to affected states, guided by the needs and priorities of affected communities. Third, efforts to address past harm must be accompanied by measures to prevent future harm. We remain concerned by any possibility of resumption of nuclear testing and reaffirm the importance of maintaining testing moratoria and advancing the entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. Co-chairs, addressing the legacy of nuclear weapons is both a humanitarian imperative and a matter of justice. We are hoping that today's meeting could sustain international attention and provide practical recommendations that strengthen victims' assistance, environmental remediation, and international cooperation while advancing our shared objective of a world free of nuclear weapons. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Indonesia for the statement and now give the floor to the representative of Philippines to be followed by the representative of Austria. Philippines, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I would like to thank the

Chairmanship and the entire work of Kazakhstan and Kiribati in convening this meeting. For decades, communities have continued to live with the consequences of nuclear weapons and use and testing. The harm did not end when the detonation stopped. It has persisted through radiation, contamination of land and water, health consequences, disrupted livelihoods, and social and psychological suffering. In many cases, these effects have extended across generations. We meet therefore not only to reflect on the past, but consider what we can do better today. The Philippines stands in solidarity with affected regions, states, and communities. Their experiences underscore several important lessons, some of which delegations have already underscored. First, victim assistance must be comprehensive and long-term. Medical care must be accompanied by psychosocial and socioeconomic support, including measures that enable affected communities to rebuild their lives and livelihoods. Second, environmental remediation must be grounded in sound science and sustained monitoring. Contaminated environments require careful assessment, appropriate remediation, and continued attention to risks that may persist long after initial cleanup efforts. Third, affected communities must be at the center of these efforts. They should be meaningfully involved. in identifying their needs, designing responses, and evaluating their implementation. Particular attention should be given to women and girls, children, indigenous peoples, and future generations. Fourth, transparency and access to information are indispensable. Communities cannot fully understand or address the consequences of nuclear use and testing without access to relevant historical, scientific, and environmental information. We therefore encourage states that have used or tested nuclear weapons to share relevant information, including the declassifying information that can contribute to victim assistance and environmental remediation. Chair, humanitarian treaties have an important role in translating these lessons into commitments. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons provides a clear legal framework for positive obligations of victim assistance and environmental remediation. as well as international cooperation and assistance. As a state party to the TPNW, the Philippines remains committed to advancing its effective implementation. These obligations complement the broader disarmament and non-proliferation architecture. The NPT has recognized, including through successive review conferences, the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons and the need to address their legacy. The Philippines has likewise consistently underscored that the onus should be on the states that conducted nuclear tests rather than on the states and communities that are victims of their reverberating impacts. The CTBT, meanwhile, represents a critical contribution to preventing further harm by prohibiting explosions and strengthening the international monitoring and verification. As co-presidents together with Sweden of the Article 14 process, the Philippines remains committed to advancing the treaty's entry into force and strengthening the global norm against nuclear testing. At the regional level, ASEAN's commitment to the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon Free Zone reflects our shared determination to prevent our region from becoming a theater for nuclear weapons and to protect our people and our environment from their consequences. Mr. Chair, translating these commitments into practical action requires sustained international cooperation. We encourage states and relevant international organizations to strengthen cooperation in independent scientific research, environmental monitoring and assessment, and the development and sharing of effective remediation practices. We also encourage greater capacity building for affected states and communities, particularly where technical, scientific, or institutional resources remain limited. the same time, programs of medical, psychosocial and socioeconomic assistance should be sustained, accessible and designed in meaningful consultation with affected communities and responsive to their evolving needs. Above all, we must ensure that the lessons of those who have endured the consequences of nuclear weapons are not lost. Addressing the legacy of nuclear weapons is an essential part of our shared responsibility to present and future generations. is also an essential part of our broader commitment to a world in which no community will again have to bear the human and environmental consequences of nuclear weapons. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the representative of Philippines for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Austria to be followed by the representative of Bangladesh. Austria, you have the floor.

Distinguished co-chairs, dear colleagues and members of civil society, Austria thanks the co-chairs Kazakhstan and Kiribati for convening the very first meeting on victim assistance and environmental remediation. And we would like to congratulate you for your dedicated leadership on an issue that is often overlooked. We welcome representatives of the civil society, in particular from organizations representing victims and affected communities. Your presence here today and your voices are key to remind us, member states, about an ethical and moral obligation not to leave affected communities behind. For Austria, disarmament has never been an abstract exercise in arms control. We view disarmament through a humanitarian lens. This conviction runs through decades of Austrian disarmament engagement. The anti-personnel mine ban convention, where Austria chaired the first review conference. the Convention on Cluster Munitions, which Austria co-initiated and which was the first disarmament treaty to establish a legal obligation on victim assistance. And with the EVIPA declaration adopted in Dublin in 2022, states committed to a holistic, integrated, gender-sensitive and non-discriminatory approach to assisting victims. Austria initiated the idea and hosted the 2019 Vienna conference that launched the negotiations. The example of explosive weapons is instructive. According to international statistics, 90% of the victims of explosive weapons in populated areas are civilians. The consequences do not end when the fighting stops. Co-chairs, as an OPCW member, Austria has supported the destruction of chemical weapons and the care of their victims, from the OPCW Trust Fund for Victims of Chemical Weapons to the Trust Fund for Syria Missions. and joined the International Partnership Against Impunity for the Use of Chemical Weapons. The same humanitarian logic lies at the heart of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. The TPNW is more than a prohibition treaty, it's a humanitarian treaty. Articles six and seven make victim assistance and environmental remediation a shared responsibility of all states parties. Victim assistance and environmental remediation are not afterthoughts to disarmament. They are essential to its credibility and its future. A disarmament regime that cares for the victims of weapons is a regime that is trusted, and a regime that is trusted is a regime that states will join and uphold. By addressing the full human cost of weapons, the immediate suffering and the long term damage to health, environment and communities, these obligations put people at the centre of the disarmament discourse. They transform disarmament from a purely technical exercise into a humanitarian endeavor, and they build the solidarity and shared responsibility that give the norm its moral and political force. In short, they are not just about repairing the past. They are about building the trust and legitimacy on which a world free from nuclear weapons depends. We look forward to continuing the discussion on victim assistance and environmental remediation during the first refcon of the TPNW this December, and I thank you.

I thank the representative of Austria for the statement and warm words addressed to the co-chairs. Now I would like to give the floor to the representative of Bangladesh, to be followed by Japan. Bangladesh, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Bangladesh welcomes the convening of this international meeting on victim assistance and environmental remediation. We would also like to welcome the participation of the affected communities. More than eight decades have passed since the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. It is really unfortunate that over 2,000 nuclear tests were conducted in different parts of the world following those tragedies. The experience of survivors and affected communities have demonstrated that the consequences of nuclear weapons transcend national borders. And the ramifications don't end when the immediate destructions subside. The humanitarian and environmental impacts can persist across generations, affecting human health, livelihoods, land, water, and ecosystems. Over the years, these lived experiences have reminded us that nuclear disarmament is not only a question of national security, It is about people, communities, human dignity, and our collective responsibility to future generations. Mr. Chair, Bangladesh remains firmly committed to the NPT as a cornerstone of the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime. Against a backdrop of heightened nuclear risks, NPT reminds us of the urgent need to rebuild trust and demonstrate tangible progress towards nuclear disarmament. The urgency of our deliberations today is further underscored by developments in the broader nuclear disarmament architecture. Earlier this year, the 11th Review Conference of the NPT concluded without a consensus outcome. Nevertheless, the victims and affected communities must be placed at the centre of the nuclear disarmament-related talks. Their lived experiences and priorities should guide the design and implementation of assistance programmes. Such assistance needs to remain accessible, inclusive and non-discriminatory, with due attention to women, children, persons with disabilities and others facing particular vulnerabilities. Environmental remediation equally requires sustained international attention. Affected States should therefore be supported in conducting scientific assessments, environmental monitoring and appropriate remediation, including through access to expertise, technology and adequate resources. Against this backdrop, the TPNW marked an important development in international disarmament efforts. Its provisions on victim assistance, environmental remediation, and international cooperation and assistance recognize that addressing the legacy of nuclear weapons must go hand in hand with preventing their future use. The Vienna Action Plan adopted at the first meeting of States Parties to the TPNW in 2022 provided a practical framework for translating these obligations into action. Today's meeting also comes at an important moment as we look towards the first review conference of TPNW later this year. The review conference will offer us an opportunity to reassess progress under the Vienna Action Plan and to further strengthen implementation of Article 6 and 7 of the Treaty. Mr. Chair, despite being situated in a nuclear-armed region, Bangladesh has chosen to remain non-nuclear. As one of the first South Asian countries, we ratified the CTBT and TPNW. We call upon the Member States towards the universalization. Bangladesh remains firmly committed to comprehensive, verifiable and irreversible nuclear disarmament. The most effective guarantee against new victims, new contaminated communities and further environmental devastation remains the total elimination of nuclear weapons. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Bangladesh for his statement. Now I invite the representative of Japan to take the floor and to be followed by Thailand. Japan, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chairs, Excellencies, and distinguished delegates and participants. Japan welcomes the convening of this international meeting on victim assistance and environmental remediation. I wish to express my sincere appreciation to you, co-chairs, for guiding our discussions. I also pay tribute to all participating states and organizations for their commitment to this important issue. Above all, Japan expresses its profound respect for and solidarity with the victims, survivors, and the communities affected by the use and testing of nuclear weapons. Japan voted in favor of General Assembly Resolution 79/60 and 80/56 related to the convening of this meeting. We welcome this important opportunity for the international community to consider how we can provide victim assistance and support environmental remediation. As the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war, Japan has long provided assistance to the victims of the atomic bombings and undertaken efforts for environmental remediation in Japan. Drawing on the experience and knowledge accumulated through these efforts, Japan has also applied them beyond its borders by actively providing assistance to victims of nuclear testing and supporting environmental remediation in affected areas. One recent example is our cooperation with Kazakhstan. In August 2025, Japan decided to provide grant aid of 1 billion and 87 million yen for medical equipment, including MRI and CT scanners, to support victims of nuclear testing. Through the provision of this equipment, Japan seeks to improve the quality of medical services and access to healthcare for people living in affected areas. Mr. Co-Chair, Japan also supports the work of the Independent Scientific Panel on the Effects of Nuclear War. The panel is tasked with examining the physical effects and societal consequences of nuclear war and their impacts on public health, global socio-economic systems, agriculture, and ecosystems. We believe that the work of the panel will contribute to promoting accurate understanding of the realities of nuclear weapon use. For Japan, promoting accurate understanding of these realities is a starting point for all measures towards nuclear disarmament. Last year marked the 80th year since the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The unwavering wish of the hibakusha is that such devastation must never be repeated. In this regard, Japan attaches great importance to visits by political leaders and senior government officials, as well as by mid-career and young leaders and youth delegations to places affected by the use or testing of nuclear weapons. Japan will promote this especially through encouraging visit to Hiroshima and Nagasaki. We also commend opportunities for them to engage directly with survivors and affected communities. Such visits and exchanges enable participants to learn firsthand about the consequences of nuclear weapons and hear directly from those who have experienced them. Japan encourages all member states to promote such visits and exchanges. We must also ensure that the stories and memories of those affected are preserved and faithfully passed on to future generations. As the number of those able to share their experiences firsthand continues to decline, these efforts are becoming ever more urgent. Japan will continue to cooperate closely with relevant states and partners in promoting accurate understanding of the realities of nuclear weapon use, providing assistance to victims, and supporting environmental remediation. Through these efforts, Japan will continue to work towards the realization of a world without nuclear weapons. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Japan for the statement. And now I give the floor to the representative of Thailand, followed to be followed by New Zealand. Thailand, you have the floor.

Thailand welcomes the convening of this timely meeting as mandated by General Assembly resolutions 7960 and 8056. the long-term humanitarian consequences and environmental degradation caused by nuclear weapons testing and use demand an urgent and united international response. In addressing the nuclear legacy, Thailand emphasizes three key priorities. First is to deliver actionable survivor-centered victim assistance and environmental remediation frameworks. As one of the first party states to the TPNW, Thailand views Article 6 and 7 as essential legal and moral obligations. Our efforts to provide practical victim support and effective environmental restoration must be based on the actual need of survivors. Thailand recognizes the disproportionate impact of nuclear weapons on women and children. Therefore, it is crucial that we developed targeted protection and assistance frameworks to mitigate the long-term harm inflicted on vulnerable communities. Second, to ensure sustainable technical and financial support, Thailand supports the establishment of an international trust fund for victim assistance and environmental remediation. We emphasize the need to engage the scientific community, affected communities, civil society and international organizations in this regard. Thailand looks forward to the discussions on the trust fund's terms of reference, guidelines, technical provisions based on the co-chairs report. Third and finally, we need to reinforce a complementary global non-proliferation and disarmament architecture. Thailand views that addressing humanitarian harm and advancing global disarmament efforts are mutually reinforcing endeavors. We should therefore ensure synergy among development instruments, be they the TPNW, NPT, CTBT, or the regional nuclear weapon free zone treaties, including the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaty, while advancing, of course, scientific study on humanitarian impacts, strengthening international humanitarian law, and reinforcing our check goal of a total elimination of nuclear weapons. Of course, as the most effective way to prevent future victims and environmental harm is, of course, to ensure that nuclear weapons are never to be tested or used again and ultimately they are to be eliminated. Thailand stand ready to work constructively with our member states and stakeholders to realize this long overdue aspiration. Thank you so much for your very kind attention.
I thank the representative of Thailand for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of New Zealand to be followed by South Africa. New Zealand, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. Excellencies, dear colleagues. New Zealand welcomes the opportunity that this one-day meeting provides to focus international attention on the legacy of nuclear weapons and states affected by their use or testing. We commend the role of two states directly affected by the legacy of nuclear testing, Kazakhstan and Kiribati, in leading this initiative. New Zealand supported United Nations Resolution 79/60 and 80/56, which led to this meeting. and is pleased to see it come to fruition. The fact that votes were called on those resolutions underlines the contrasting perspectives on aspects of the international community's efforts to address nuclear legacies. New Zealand's views on assistance and remediation with respect to nuclear weapons use or testing are inextricably linked to their poisonous legacy in the Pacific. From the late 1940s to 1996, nuclear tests conducted in the Pacific region by nuclear-armed states generated impacts on people and the environment that continue to be felt today. Whatever the purported security benefits to the nuclear powers concerned of the nuclear weapons that were tested, the human and environmental costs fell disproportionately on small communities distant from metropolitan areas and perhaps consequently seem to be of marginal concern. Those costs of nuclear testing were diverse. While some impacts were undoubtedly short-term, others have been intergenerational. Besides physical and psychosocial health concerns, they caused lasting environmental harm, including contamination, displacement, and disconnection of communities from their land. loss of livelihoods, and enduring feelings of injustice. The effects of climate change, such as sea level rise, on the structural integrity of nuclear material storage sites present new concerns. This lived experience of nuclear legacies has shaped responses and attitudes towards nuclear weapons ever since for states in the Pacific region, including New Zealand. We and many others have argued including in our submissions to the Secretary-General's report on addressing the legacy of nuclear weapons in 2024, that it makes sense to situate assistance to survivors and environmental remediation within the broader nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation agenda. Until nuclear weapons are eliminated, there is always the possibility of future victims and environmental contamination. Clearly, we are still a long way from achieving a world free of nuclear weapons. Nevertheless, we commend the Secretary-General's report as a step in the right direction, including his recommendations. One key recommendation in his report was for serious consideration to be given to establishing mechanisms for international cooperation and assistance. This is a topic that has subsequently been raised in a range of international forums, including in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty context, and pursued in the treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons. Another recommendation in the report was that the United Nations system should, where appropriate, support efforts to deepen understanding of the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons and facilitate the provision of international cooperation and assistance. We urge all states to engage in these efforts moving forward. Today's discussion could become a critical moment in a conversation that we hope will, in time, deliver tangible results for those still living with nuclear legacies. I thank you.
I thank the representative of New Zealand for the statement. Now I give the floor to the representative of South Africa, to be followed by Marshall Islands. South Africa, you have the floor.

Thank you, co-chairs. South Africa welcomes the initiative calling for this important international meeting to be convened. It is a timely contribution to discussions to address the legacy of nuclear weapons through the provision of victim assistance and environmental remediation to member states affected by the use or testing of nuclear weapons. Co-chairs, it is regrettable that 80 years after nuclear weapons were first tested and used, these horrific weapons continue to pose an existential threat to humanity. The experiences of individuals and states affected by the testing of nuclear weapons, with thousands of explosive nuclear tests being conducted around the globe, bear testament to the horrors of nuclear weapons. Nuclear weapons are cruel and indiscriminate. They wreak havoc and cause massive, unacceptable loss of life, long-term damage to the environment, and have severe health consequences. It must be emphasized that national boundaries are blurred when it comes to the fallout from any nuclear weapon use. The understanding and awareness of the catastrophic impact of a nuclear weapon of a nuclear weapon detonation and the continued risks for such a detonation, whether by accident, miscalculation or design, have contributed to enduring or ensuring that humanitarian considerations can no longer be ignored. These humanitarian consequences are substantiated by new scientific evidence. This growing body of research confirms that the effects of a nuclear detonation are more severe cascading, long-lasting and complex than previously understood. It involves short and long-term damage to the environment, sustainable development, the global economy, food security and the health of current and future generations. It also includes the disproportionate impact that nuclear weapons have on women and girls, including as a result of ionizing radiation, as well as on infants, and children given their particular vulnerability to the effects of nuclear weapons. Co-chairs, the catastrophic humanitarian consequences and risks associated with nuclear weapons underpin the moral and ethical imperatives for nuclear disarmament and the urgency of achieving and maintaining a nuclear weapon-free world. Concerns about the catastrophic humanitarian and environmental impact of nuclear weapons have been with us since the first use of these weapons. These concerns were the motivating factor for the establishment of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the NPT, and they remain a motivating factor in insisting that all of its provisions are fully implemented, including disarmament. Similarly, The Treaty for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, the TPNW, is premised on the fundamental principle of humanity and the ethical imperatives for nuclear disarmament. The TPNW demonstrates growing support for humanitarian efforts to take decisive action against nuclear weapons, and its significance in relation to Article 6 of the NPT cannot be overemphasized. It is unacceptable that decades after the use or testing of nuclear weapons, many affected communities still await assistance and environmental remediation. The TPNW States Parties and signatory States are doing their part by advancing the implementation of the positive obligations of the TPNW, including through the development of mechanisms to facilitate victim assistance and environmental remediation.
